summary: Describes how the NIST Secure Hash Standard family of algorithms can be used with the built-in cryptographic authentication of OSPF version 2. It updates, but does not replace, the mechanism from RFC 2328. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5709 adds SHA-based authentication to Open Shortest Path First version 2 (OSPFv2). Routers use a shared key and a hashed message authentication code (HMAC) to check each packet.

subtitle: How OSPFv2 uses HMAC with SHA algorithms to authenticate routing packets.

tldr.problem: OSPFv2 cryptographic authentication used Keyed-MD5, while operators asked to use algorithms from the NIST Secure Hash Standard.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC applies HMAC-SHA algorithms to the existing OSPFv2 cryptographic-authentication process. A shared key and packet produce a digest that is attached to each packet.
tldr.outcome: Implementations MUST support HMAC-SHA-256. RFC 5709 updates RFC 2328 and was later updated by RFC 7474.

today: RFC 5709 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2328 and was updated by RFC 7474. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why OSPFv2 Adds HMAC-SHA
sections.content:
Open Shortest Path First version 2 (OSPFv2) already defined cryptographic authentication using Keyed-MD5. RFC 5709 adds authentication using the Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA) family in Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC) mode, in response to operator requests.

This document applies only to Authentication Type 2, Cryptographic Authentication. It updates the authentication mechanism in RFC 2328; it does not replace or deprecate that RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Open Shortest Path First version 2 (OSPFv2) could already authenticate packets with a shared secret and Keyed-MD5. This RFC adds a way to use SHA-based HMAC with the same overall process.

sections.title: What the Routers Share
sections.content:
Routers on a common network configure a shared secret key. For each OSPF packet, the sender uses the key and packet contents to calculate a message digest, then appends the digest to the packet. The key itself is not sent in cleartext.

The packet carries a KeyID so the receiver can select the matching security association. The association holds the key, algorithm, identifier, and times for starting and stopping packet generation and acceptance. OSPFv2 does not provide an in-band method to create or manage these associations.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers on the same network must have matching key information. The packet carries a key identifier and a digest, allowing the receiver to choose the right key and check the packet.

sections.title: Supported Algorithms and Digest Creation
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support HMAC-SHA-256. They SHOULD support HMAC-SHA-1 and Keyed-MD5, and MAY support HMAC-SHA-384 and HMAC-SHA-512. Operators must be able to configure any supported algorithm with any configured KeyID.

For HMAC-SHA, the sender prepares the key, computes an inner hash over the packet and an outer hash over that result, then places the outer hash in the authentication trailer. The digest length follows the selected algorithm: SHA-1 uses 20 bytes, SHA-256 32 bytes, SHA-384 48 bytes, and SHA-512 64 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Every implementation must support HMAC-SHA-256, while support for other listed algorithms has different requirement levels. The sender calculates the digest in two hash steps, and larger digests add more bytes to the packet.

sections.title: Changing Keys and Checking Packets
sections.content:
The KeyID lets a receiver find the security association for a packet without trying every configured key. To make a key change smoothly, the acceptance window for a new key SHOULD begin before the router starts generating packets with it, and the old key SHOULD remain accepted after generation with it stops.

The receiver saves the received digest, calculates the expected digest, and compares the two. The sequence number follows RFC 2328 procedures. Replaying a captured packet can disrupt routing if its sequence number becomes valid again; RFC 5709 notes that automated OSPF key management had not been standardized when it was published.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can overlap the acceptance times for old and new keys while changing keys. Authentication does not prevent every attack: a nearby attacker may replay a packet if its sequence number becomes valid again.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
HMAC authentication shows that the sender knew the shared security association, but symmetric cryptography does not identify which router sent the packet. The RFC says routing data needs authentication but not confidentiality, and notes that IPsec or digital signatures are alternatives.

RFC 5709 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2328. The batch metadata says RFC 7474 later updated this document; it has not been obsoleted.
sections.plainLanguage: A valid digest shows that a sender knew the shared key, but it does not prove which router sent the packet. RFC 7474 later updated this specification, which remains un-obsoleted according to the batch metadata.
